defects.description: Portal API containers (AWS Fargate) run in a private subnet without a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints in the VPC, leaving private tasks with no network path to pull container images or reach Amazon Cognito and Amazon CloudWatch.
The architecture omits a backend database or persistent data tier in private subnets for customer banking data, only storing static web assets and CloudTrail logs in S3.
Application Load Balancer — Availability Zone B (N6) has no outgoing edge to Portal API containers (N7), and Portal API containers are placed only in Private application subnet A.

reviews.summary: Design A provides a strong edge and audit security posture with CloudFront OAC, WAF, end-to-end TLS, Cognito TOTP MFA, and Object Lock CloudTrail storage, but omits a customer database tier and lacks a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints for private Fargate tasks.

defects.description: A single NAT Gateway is placed only in Public subnet A while Portal API tasks run in Private app subnet B; if Availability Zone A fails, private tasks in Availability Zone B lose outbound internet access to Amazon Cognito and container registries, violating R17.
Application Load Balancer (Availability Zone B nodes) (N6), AWS Shield (N2), and AWS KMS (N12) have no edges, and Portal API tasks (N9) is missing an egress edge to the NAT Gateway.
Portal web app tasks (N8) are placed only in Availability Zone A and Portal API tasks (N9) are placed only in Availability Zone B rather than deploying both services across both Availability Zones.

reviews.summary: Design B covers all functional and security requirements including a KMS-encrypted Multi-AZ Aurora database in dedicated private data subnets and end-to-end TLS, with its main weakness being a single-AZ NAT Gateway and several unconnected diagram nodes.

defects.description: Configuring the Application Load Balancer to authenticate all shopper requests against an Amazon Cognito user pool before forwarding to Web API containers blocks anonymous e-commerce shoppers from browsing product pages or searching, and the edge direction from Cognito to ALB is reversed.

EventBridge scheduled rules have a minimum resolution of 1 minute, so polling the outbox on an EventBridge schedule cannot reliably guarantee that price updates appear in OpenSearch within one minute once polling delay, execution, and index refresh latency are combined.
Web API containers (Fargate) run in a private subnet without a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints in the VPC, preventing tasks from pulling container images or reaching public AWS endpoints.
Indexer failure queue (N11) has no connected edges, and the ALB, Fargate tasks, RDS Proxy, and Aurora are placed only in Availability Zone A.

reviews.summary: Design A uses an appropriate Aurora, RDS Proxy, and OpenSearch core, but forces Cognito login at the ALB for public shoppers, relies on 1-minute EventBridge polling that can miss the 1-minute price SLA, and leaves its DLQ and private subnet egress unconnected.

defects.description: Only a single NAT Gateway is provisioned in Public subnet A (and has no connected edges), creating a single-AZ point of failure for private subnet outbound connectivity if Availability Zone A fails.
Route 53 is modeled inline in the HTTPS request path (Shoppers -> Route 53 -> CloudFront over HTTPS) rather than as a DNS lookup service.
While the Lambda index updater invalidates ElastiCache (Valkey) on product changes, CloudFront edge cache TTL or invalidation is not specified to prevent stale prices on edge-cached product pages.

reviews.summary: Design B is a well-architected e-commerce search solution combining CloudFront and ElastiCache Valkey for read-heavy product pages with a DMS-to-Kinesis-to-Lambda CDC pipeline that updates OpenSearch and invalidates cache within the one-minute window.

defects.description: Edges from API tasks A to Aurora and ElastiCache are typed as read while edges from API tasks B are typed as write, even though the edge labels state that both task groups read and write data.
API tasks (Fargate) B is missing an edge to CloudWatch, and the helper Lambda function used by Secrets Manager to rotate private Aurora credentials is omitted.

reviews.summary: Design A delivers a complete, genuinely Multi-AZ container architecture on AWS Fargate with redundant per-AZ NAT Gateways for third-party payment calls, Multi-AZ Aurora PostgreSQL and ElastiCache, and automated credential rotation via Secrets Manager.

defects.description: Amazon API Gateway REST API (apiType: REST) is wired directly to an Internal ALB (which is also mistakenly placed in Public Subnet 1); API Gateway REST APIs require a VPC Link connected to a Network Load Balancer for private integrations and cannot target an Internal ALB directly.

A single NAT Gateway is placed in Public Subnet 1 (Availability Zone 1); if Availability Zone 1 fails, Fargate tasks lose outbound internet connectivity to the third-party payments API, violating the Multi-AZ requirement.
Availability Zone 2 contains no resources at all, Cognito User Pool and CloudWatch have no edges, and Secrets Manager has no edge to Fargate Tasks to supply rotated database credentials.

reviews.summary: Design B contains critical architectural flaws, including a non-working direct integration from an API Gateway REST API to an Internal ALB placed in a public subnet, a single-AZ NAT Gateway that breaks payment calls during an AZ outage, and an empty second Availability Zone.

preference.why: Design B includes the required KMS-encrypted database tier in dedicated private data subnets along with NAT egress and end-to-end TLS, whereas Design A omits any customer data store and lacks NAT or VPC endpoints for private Fargate tasks.

Design B uses a streaming CDC pipeline (DMS to Kinesis to Lambda) with ElastiCache Valkey invalidation and DLQ handling that reliably meets the sub-minute price update requirement while keeping shopping anonymous, whereas Design A blocks shoppers with ALB Cognito authentication and uses 1-minute EventBridge polling.

Design A properly distributes ALB nodes, Fargate tasks, and redundant NAT Gateways across both Availability Zones with Multi-AZ Aurora and ElastiCache, while Design B uses an invalid API Gateway REST-to-Internal-ALB integration in a public subnet and a single-AZ NAT Gateway.
